Which scale for the violation?

Source: vignettes/articles/gamma-scale.Rmd
gamma-scale.Rmd

A violation of the exclusion restriction is a number, γ, and a number needs a unit. In a linear model there is only one: γ is the direct effect of the instrument on the outcome. In a probit there are three natural ones, and apexog lets you use any of them through gunits (R) or gunits() (Stata). Internally the violation always enters the model the same way, as an offset z’γ in the probit index.

The three scales

The latent index (gunits = "latent", the default; synonym "index"). γ is a coefficient in the index of the main probit. That probit includes the control function, and it normalizes the variance of the error conditional on the control function to one. This is the scale of the offset itself, so no conversion is made. One unit of γ moves the probability of the outcome by roughly the average density of the index, mφ, per unit of the instrument; apexog prints mφ in the first “Scale” line.

Probability points (gunits = "pr"). γ is the direct effect of the instrument on the probability that y = 1, per unit of the instrument (0.02 is two percentage points). apexog divides every value you give by mφ from the baseline fit (a variance by mφ2). This is the scale on which plausexog states the violation when it is run on a binary outcome, as a linear probability model, so it is the scale to use when you compare the two commands for the same belief. It is also the scale on which most people find it easiest to say how large a direct effect could plausibly be.

The structural latent scale (gunits = "structural"). γ is a coefficient in the structural equation y* = x’β + dδ + z’γ + ε with the total error variance normalized to one, the way latent-variable models are usually written and simulated. With an endogenous d, part of the error is explained by the control function, so the probit index measures in units of the smaller conditional standard deviation σ̃ = sd(ε | control function). apexog estimates σ̃ = (1 + bcf’ Var(ĉ) bcf)−1/2 from the baseline fit and divides every value by it; the second “Scale” line reports it.

The structural conversion is derived for a linear first stage, where the control function estimates the first-stage error. With a probit, fractional probit or Poisson first stage it does not apply: in simulations the structural γ enters the index essentially unscaled. Do not combine gunits = "structural" with those first stages; state the violation on the index or in probability points instead. apexog accepts the combination but prints a warning.

Even with a linear first stage the conversion divides by the baseline σ̃, which is exact only as γ shrinks to zero. With one continuous endogenous regressor and one instrument, a structural value has a unique index-scale counterpart only below |πz|/σv in absolute value (the first-stage coefficient of the instrument over the first-stage residual standard deviation). The output reports that limit (gs_max; in Stata e(gs_max)) and warns when the range or the prior draws reach it. The results themselves are not changed.

The same belief, three ways

In the example data mφ = 0.209 and σ̃ = 0.834. A direct effect of ±0.10 on the latent index is therefore about ±0.0209 in probability and ±0.0834 on the structural scale. Stated in those units, the three calls run the same grid and give the same bounds:

library(apexog)
data(promotion)
f <- promoted ~ tenure + manager
e <- training ~ subsidy

index <- apexog(f, endog = e, data = promotion, gmin = -0.10, gmax = 0.10,
                grid = 5, verbose = FALSE)
m <- index$mphi
s <- index$stilde
c(m_phi = m, sigma_tilde = s)
#>       m_phi sigma_tilde 
#>   0.2090548   0.8342901

pr <- apexog(f, endog = e, data = promotion, gunits = "pr",
             gmin = -0.10 * m, gmax = 0.10 * m, grid = 5, verbose = FALSE)
st <- apexog(f, endog = e, data = promotion, gunits = "structural",
             gmin = -0.10 * s, gmax = 0.10 * s, grid = 5, verbose = FALSE)

rbind(index = confint(index), pr = confint(pr), structural = confint(st))
#>               lower     upper
#> training 0.09709467 0.1904491
#> training 0.09709467 0.1904491
#> training 0.09709467 0.1904491

The grid stored in the result is always on the latent index; grid_pr holds the exact probability-scale value of each grid point:

cbind(index$grid["g_subsidy"], index$grid_pr)
#>   g_subsidy gpr_subsidy
#> 1     -0.10 -0.02090548
#> 2     -0.05 -0.01045274
#> 3      0.00  0.00000000
#> 4      0.05  0.01045274
#> 5      0.10  0.02090548

Why the scale matters

The conversions are not cosmetic. If you have a belief on the structural scale and enter it as if it were on the index, the violation you assume is too small by the factor σ̃. Under the local-to-zero method the interval is then too narrow: with a wide prior its coverage approaches 2Φ(z σ̃) − 1 instead of the nominal level (about 0.88 instead of 0.95 at an endogeneity correlation of 0.6 in simulations). Stating the belief in probability points avoids the question of which latent scale is meant.

Exact probability scale

The conversion gunits = "pr" is a first-order one: it uses mφ from the model with γ = 0. apexog also reports, at every refit, the exact probability-scale value of each instrument’s violation in the model refitted at that violation:

  • for a 0/1 instrument, the average change in the probability of the outcome when the instrument switches from 0 to 1;
  • for any other instrument, the average derivative, mean φ(η)·γ.

The two agree for small violations. They can differ by several percent for a large violation of a 0/1 instrument when the outcome is close to 0 or 1. With a linear first stage, as many instruments as endogenous regressors and a continuous instrument they coincide exactly, as in the example above. The values are printed beside each range (“exact Pr scale”) and stored in grid_pr (UCI) and sims$gamma_pr (LTZ); in Stata in e(grid_pr) and e(gamma_pr_sim).

Both factors describe the baseline fit

mφ and σ̃ are computed from the model with γ = 0. When the true violation is not zero that model is misspecified, so both are properties of that fit rather than structural constants; the conversion is exact as γ shrinks to zero.
